On the one hand, there are those, like Detterman, who view the evidence on transferand shake their heads in utter despair, claiming that cases of signi "cant transfer are `rarer than volcanic eruptions and large earthquakes aand as di $cult to predict (1993,p

On the other hand, there are those, like Bereiter (1995), who argue for a lessgrandiose notion of transfer, and who, thus, see clear and frequent evidence of transferin the learning of fundamental processes (e.g., reading) and in the application ofconceptual learning across contexts

In reconciling the contrasts in these two perspectives, Gentner and Markman (1997) o!er their own comparison, abandoning Detterman 's colorful `volcanoes and earth- quakes ametaphor in favor of one referencing comets and planets

According to Gentner and Markman, the normatively signi "cant insights that Detterman (1993) describes are like comets *riveting, brilliant, and rare #ashes of perspicacity that streak through one 's mind
In contrast, there are those more prosaic, highly predict- able, and less dramatic occasions of transfer that oftentimes go unnoticed
These,according to Gentner and Markman, are like planets that move about the heavenswith predictable and quiet regularity

Despite their disparate appearances and variedbehaviors, as Gentner and Markman are quick to point out, both comets and planetsare regulated by similar fundamental principles and both are central astronomicphenomena
Transfer, like comets and planets, takes multiple forms with di !ering probabilities of occurrence

Yet, whether one is on the low road (i.e., literal similarity, re #exive action, and well-practiced tasks) or the high road (i.e., abstraction of principles, e!ortful processing, increased complexity, and novelty) to transfer (Salomon & Perki- ns, 1989), the fundamental processes remain relatively consistent
As noted, transferinvolves the process of applying one 's prior knowledge or experience to some new situation

Further, the tremendous range of opinions within the psychological andeducational communities as to the meaning, nature, and likelihood of transfer not-withstanding, there are at least "ve defensible generalizations about transfer
Generalizations about transfer Transfer is an essential aspect of competent performance in any complex domain

There is ample evidence in the literature that highly competent learners, experts (andpossibly some professors) regularly perform tasks for which they have never beendirectly trained (Chi, Feltovich & Glaser, 1981; Corkill & Fager, 1995; Lerda,Garzunel & Therme, 1996)
For example, a skilled professor might use her under-standing of social hierarchies as a mechanism for understanding the societal workingsand hierarchy of various ant colonies
Similarly, a learner who is competent inphysical science will apply his knowledge of pulleys, levers, and fulcrums to ease theburden of moving heavy boxes out of his garage and into a truck
However, the samecannot be said for learners who are less competent or only acclimated in their "elds
As James (1890) so duly noted, such individuals do not possess the excess con- sciousness required to grapple with the transfer of knowledge

competent science learner must expend his cognitive energies on grasping the theory behind centrifugal force rather than using that information to understand why he doesnot fall out of a loopty-loop roller coaster

Further, our research would suggest thatthese acclimated learners also lack the strategic ability and interest requisite forcarrying out transfer in a complex domain (e.g., Alexander, Jetton & Kulikowich,1996; Alexander, Murphy, Woods, Duhon & Parker, 1997)
Thus, it would appearthat transfer is a critical dimension of able performance
Moreover, even if Detter-man's admonition *`if you want people to learn something, teach it to them a(1993,p
21)*were heeded, it is impossible to convey even the most basic of academic knowledge and skills in all their potential iterations
No teacher, regardless of howdedicated,e !ective, or creative, can deal with the time demands and complexity (to say nothing of the tedium) that such instruction would necessitate
Transfer of schooled knowledge and procedures occurs far less often than educators and educational researchers would hope
The literature is replete with testimonials to the relative ine !ectiveness of `training for transfer astudies (e.g., Brown, Collins & Duguid, 1989; Salomon & Perkins, 1989)
That is to say, students who are taught todoXunder conditions Yfrequently fail to do Xunder conditionsZ
Suppose, for example, a "fth grader is taught how to represent a one-step comparison word problem graphically as a way to decide the appropriate algorithm to employ
Whenencountering word problems that involve multiple steps or alternative functions,however, the child does not attempt to transform the linguistic problem into graphic form
When studies have been successful at producing transfer, it is far more likely to have been neartransfer than fartransfer
For instance, Singley and Anderson (1989) reviewed the theoretical and empirical transfer literature from Thorndike to thepresent and found very little documentation of far or general transfer
They con-cluded: `Besides the spate of negative evidence, there has been no positive evidence of general transfer besides a few highly questionable studies a(p

In general, training studies tend to demonstrate transfere !ects when: (a) researchers or practitioners target near transfer tasks rather than far transfer tasks; (b) the structural similaritiesare still rather apparent or literal; or, (c) helpful hints and cues prompt students to usetrained knowledge or skills (Detterman, 1993)

In addition, Perkins (1992) and others (e.g., Campione, Shapiro & Brown, 1995; Holyoak & Thagard, 1997) have insisted that successful transfer is dependent ona sense of purpose in the content to be learned, as well as the situations in which theknowledge can and should be transferred
That is to say, students should be engagedin meaningful, problem-based activities for which the knowledge and skills acquiredare means for accomplishment rather than ends in themselves
Further, studentsshould be shown how the knowledge and skills they attain in one problem-basedsituation have utility in other relevant contexts
Such conditions are often di $cult to achieve in classrooms as they are presently con "gured

Therefore, even if an optimistic outlook on the occurrence of transfer is assumed, the situation is still far from optimal.There is much more that can and should be done to create a disposition towardtransfer among learners (Bereiter, 1995)
Transfer is more apt to occur when the learning en vironment is intentionally orches- trated to encourage cross-situation and cross-domain transfer and rewards suche worts.P.A

Among the character- istics that are regularly discussed under this rubric are adequate time devoted totraining, explicitness of instructional content, attention to basic problem-solvingprocedures or strategies, multiple and varied opportunities for transfer, and mindfulre#ection and abstraction of the materials to be taught (e.g., McKeough, Lupart & Marini, 1995; Pressley, 1995)

Still, as noted, these reasonable characteristics havenot often resulted in instructional outcomes that are readily transferable to more thanthe most similar of tasks or that endure long after training terminates (Detterman,1993)

These disappointing "ndings underscore that teaching for transfer is very demanding and requires a long-term instructional commitment, adequate resourcesand learning tasks, as well as knowledgeable and dedicated teachers (Cox, 1997;Marini & Genereux, 1995)
Beyond these reasonable components, transfer seems to require a level of encultura- tion into the domains from which concepts and problems arise (Greeno, Moore& Smith, 1993)
Yet, the nature of schooling is customarily such that students do nothave the opportunity to develop a realistic or deep sense of the academic domains thatare the mainstay of formal education

Accordingly, because of their piecemeal orpatchwork understanding of such "elds as mathematics, history, or science, students continue to treat concepts or procedures in a fragmented or unduly constrainedmanner (Byrnes, 1996)
In essence, students see each task as a separate exercise, anisolated performance event where maximum points are often earned merely forduplicating what was taught in just the manner instructed
Moreover, since the failureto transfer is rarely associated with lower grades in classrooms, students feel littlecompunction when transfer is not evidenced
In its most general sense, analogical reasoning is the ability to establish relationships between two seeminglydissimilar entities (Corkill & Fager, 1995; Schunn & Dunbar, 1996)

Detterman 's (1993) likening of transfer to volcanic eruptions is an illustration of analogicalthinking in that it entails comparing ideas from one domain (psychology) to conceptsin another, quite varied, domain (geophysics)

The value of such a process is that itallows individuals to reconceptualize and reposition more abstract or novel ideas (e.g.,transfer) in terms of concepts that are perhaps more concrete and more familiar (e.g.,volcanoes)

For this process to worke !ectively (if at all), such analogical reasoning requires that individuals possess conceptual understanding of both the source andtarget domains (e.g., psychology and geophysics)
Further, these domains must belinked through certain relational processes (e.g., inferring or mapping; Pirolli& Recker, 1994; Sternberg & Rifkin, 1979)

The investigations of various researchers give credence to this view that the processes underlying conceptual transfer correspond directly to those required toreason analogically (Gentner & Markman, 1997; Reeves & Weisberg, 1994)
So muchso, in fact, that many researchers investigate transfer as though it were a special case ofanalogical reasoning (e.g., Kolodner, 1997; Reeves & Weisberg, 1993)

Certainly, it canbe argued that if learners fail to see the similarities between particular tasks orcontexts, then it is improbable that they will engage in the mindful transfer ofconceptual or procedural knowledge across tasks or contexts.564P.A
The seeds of transfer are multifaceted, encompassing aspects of the learner, the content, and the context

In considering the challenge of teaching for transfer, Marini and Genereux (1995) asked the thought-provoking question of whether educators shouldfocus theire !orts on tasks, learners, or contexts in their instruction
They summarily state that `taking all three into account when designing instruction is most advisable a (p
Even thoughtfully designed instructional programs cannot hope to succeedoften or well unless they attend simultaneously to the learner , the content , and the context

This claim is based on our research in academic development and analogical reasoning, as well as on the informative studies of others (e.g., Ackerman & Hegges-tad, 1997; Goska & Ackerman, 1996; Lupart, 1995)
Furthermore, the interplayamong particular learner attributes establishes the fertile ground for transfer and forthe analogical thought that underlies that transfer
In the discussion that follows,certain learner, content, and context variables that build the foundation for transferare discussed brie #y

Identifying the seeds of transfer For the past "ve years, the authors have focused their energies on understanding the transformations that occur in students as they engage in domain-speci "c learning
One outcome of this research is the model of domain learning or MDL (see Alexander,1997)

In the MDL, the systematic changes that individuals undergo as a result offormal learning in a domain (e.g., physics, history, or reading) are theorized to occur inthree stages: acclimation, competency, and pro "ciency/expertise

The distinctions among acclimated, competent, and pro "cient learners are predicated on changes in their subject-matter knowledge, their situational and individual interests, as well astheir general strategic (cognitive and metacognitive) processing
These same dimen-sions of knowledge, interest, and strategic processing guide our examination oftransfer, as well

Stages of domain learning Learners in acclimation have limited and fragmented knowledge of the domain (Chi et al., 1981), including declarative (what), procedural (how), and conditional (when andwhere) understanding (Paris, Lipson & Wixson, 1983; Ryle, 1949)

Further, theirinterests are relegated more by the aspects of the immediate situation or context (i.e.,situational interest; Schiefele, 1992) than to any enduring, personal identi "cation with or valuing of the domain (i.e., individual interest; Hidi, 1990)
In addition, theirunfamiliarity with the domain means that they encounter many problems that arenovel or complex for them
Thus, they must rely heavily on general cognitive andmetacognitive strategies to aid them in their learning and performance
However,their lack of relevant subject-matter knowledge also means that their strategic pro-cessing is often ine !ective or ine $cient (Alexander & Judy, 1988)
Competent learners, by comparison, not only have acquired quantitatively more domain knowledge than acclimated learners, but that knowledge is also moreP.A
That is to say, the subject-matter knowledge of competent learners is coherently organized around key domain con-cepts and principles

Moreover, competent learners manifest an increasing interest orinvestment in the domain and its related topics, and are simultaneously less dependenton situationally interesting dimensions in the immediate context to motivate theirlearning and development

Finally, through the process of enculturation, problemstypical of the academic domains become more routine for competent learners, allow-ing for a moree $cient interplay between domain-speci "c and general strategic processing during this stage
Lastly, for the few who achieve pro "ciency, there is a tremendous breadth and depth of subject-matter knowledge
In essence, pro "cient individuals contribute new knowledge to their "eld, transforming that domain in some fashion
Also, experts have a powerful and abidinginterest in the domain and identify strongly with the community of practice

Inaddition, because these experts are pushing the boundaries of their domain and areengaged in problem formulation, they show an increased employment of generalcognitive and metacognitive strategies over competent learners

However, unlikeacclimated learners who often rely on lower-order or surface-level strategies (e.g.,rereading or rehearsal), pro "cient learners tend to use more higher-order strategies (e.g., synthesis or summarization) that allow for a depth of processing (Alexander,Graham & Harris, 1998a)
Among the various strategies studied is the fundamentalability to establish relationships across seemingly unrelated phenomena or analogicalreasoning (Sternberg & Rifkin, 1979)

Domain-speci xc analogical reasoning Our study of analogical reasoning has focused primarily on the ability to solve classic domain-speci "c analogy problems (Alexander, Jetton & Kulikowich, 1996; Alexander & Murphy, 1998b)

The solution of such domain-speci "c analogy problems requires not only an understanding of underlying cognitive processes, but also a bodyof domain-speci "c knowledge, as well as a willingness to engage ine !ortful process- ing
These problems are of the form A:B::C:D, and consist of terms drawn froma speci"c academic domain

Two examples of these problems from the "elds of human biology and educational psychology, respectively, are red blood cells:erythrocytes:: leucocytes:white blood cells , and Pavlov:classical conditioning::Skinner:operant condi- tioning
Given that analogical reasoning and transfer are such similar processes, this research can broaden our understanding of transfer and the conditions that promotesuch thinking
Pro xles of academic achie vement From research on domain-speci "c learning, diverse student pro "les associated with academic achievement and emerging learner competence have been identi "ed
These pro"les bear a strong resemblance to others described in the literature on student achievement (e.g., Recker & Pirolli, 1995; Renkl, 1997)
particularly relevant to this discussion the external criterion variable used to validate student pro "les was performance on a domain-speci "c analogy task (Alexander & Murphy, 1998b)

Speci "cally, after students participated in a semester of instruction in educational psychology, they formed four distinct clusters that di !ered signi "cantly with regard to domain-speci "c analogical reasoning ability
The four clusters were labeled the learning oriented (LO), strong knowledge (SK),e !ortful processors (EP), and nonstrategic reader (NR)
Students in the LO cluster ( n"94) displayed high knowledge and high interest in the domain and employed deeper-level strategies (e.g., summarizing or determiningmain idea) during text processing
LO students also received the highest scores on thedomain-speci "c analogy task at posttest
By comparison, students in the SK cluster (n"39) were signi "cantly less interested and less strategically engaged in the domain than those in the LO cluster
They were also lesse !ective than LO students at learning from a demanding domain-speci "c reading task
Still, their scores on the domain- speci"c analogy task, while lower than LO students at posttest, were not statistically di!erent

It is important to note, however, that SK students began the semester with signi "cantly more domain-related knowledge than students in the other three clusters, and apparently relied on this pre-existing knowledge to carry them throughthe term
The EP ( n"76) and the NR ( n"120) clusters encompassed our less academically successful students

Those in the EP group were distinct in their low domain know-ledge scores, their moderate domain interest, and their moderate level of performanceon the text-processing and domain-speci "c analogy tasks

This cluster, however, evidenced the most strategice !ort during text processing, although much of that e!ort involved rather surface-level strategies (e.g., rereading parts of the text or changing rate of reading)
Ine !ect, this learner pro "le was unique in the amount of e!ort exerted for a limited academic payo !

Finally, those in the NR cluster, the largest grouping of students at semester 's end, garnered only a moderate level of domain knowledge from instruction, had onlya moderate level of interest in the content, engaged in less strategic processing, and,not surprisingly, recalled the least from the text-processing task
Performance on thedomain-speci "c analogy measure was similarly rated as low to moderate
Based on this and other related research, there are three primary ingredients that contribute to students 'academic achievement that con "gure in di !erent ways over the course of domain learning
Moreover, students who show the greatest growthtoward domain competence and perform best on domain-speci "c analogy tasks exhibit high levels of all three of these ingredients
Should any one of these compo-nents be weakly developed, students 'academic progress over time could well be jeopardized
These students,like Renkl 's (1997) anticipative reasoners, seem to rely heavily on an existing base of knowledge to carry them, despite limited interest and investment in the domain

Itremains doubtful, however, whether this initial base of domain knowledge wouldprove su $cient to propel students into competence once they move beyond such an initial foray and into more advanced domain exploration.P.A

This con "guration of knowledge, strategic processing, and interest came into play again in an investigation of error patterns on domain-speci "c analogy measures (Alexander, Murphy & Kulikowich, 1998)
In this study, the emphasis went beyondglobal judgments of right and wrong to the information conveyed in students ' incorrect responses to analogy problems
To guide this analysis, a hierarchical errormodel devised by Alexander (1990) for classic domain-speci "c analogy problems of the form A:B::C:
In this model, the lowest forms of errors (Category 1, NoResponse; Category 2, Repetition) were indicative of limited domain and strategyknowledge
That is, students who committed these types of errors scored low onmeasures of domain knowledge and strategic processing
Commission of such errors,especially No Response errors, also seemed related to limited student engagement ore!ort
The highest forms of errors (Category 5, Domain Speci "c; Category 6, Target Variant), by comparison, were associated with relatively high levels of domain andstrategy knowledge
Another interesting result was that the types of errors to which individual students gravitated were very consistent (Experiment 1, Alexander et al., 1998a)
In fact, fornearly two-thirds of the sixth graders studied, 50% or more of their errors fell ina single-error category

Thus, the in #uence of domain knowledge, strategic processing, and motivation carried well beyond the raw score students received on a domain-speci"c analogy task to the types of mistakes they committed

Further, these errors were patterned and were di !erentially indicative of respondents 'domain knowledge, strategic processing ability, and seemingly their motivations for task performance.Based on these studies, domain knowledge, strategic processing, and motivation (e.g.,interest) underlie competent performance in academic domains, including the abilityto transfer knowledge and skills within and across that domain (i.e., analogicalreasoning)

Recognizing potential instructional barriers to transfer Elsewhere the authors have written of the negative conditions within schools that seem to impede students 'development of competence in academic domains, and, with it, their ability to engage in transfer (Alexander & Murphy, 1998a,b; Alexander,Murphy & Woods, 1996)
These conditions function as impediments because theyinterfere with students 'ability to construct a rich base of domain knowledge, and to devise or employ general strategies for deeper processing
The speci "c conditions are: mention- ing versus teaching, instructional enabling, and decontextualized instruction
Mentioning versus teaching Durkin (1978 }1979) admonished the educational community for their failure to provide meaningful reading instruction to elementary students
Speci "cally, in their e!orts to `cover the content a, teachers invested far too little time exploring important knowledge and strategies richly and deeply
Sadly, there is little reason to assume that the pattern Durkin observed 20 years ago has improved
If anything, theamount of content to be covered has only multiplied in the past two decades
The problem of super "cial treatment of subject matter is not new, of course
In How We Think , Dewey (1910/1991) decried that: `In school, amassing information always tends to escape from the ideal of wisdom or good judgment
&Covering the ground 'is the primary necessity; the nurture of the mind a bad second a(p

Questions have also been raised about the concepts that teachers emphasize (or even mention) inclassrooms and whether central domain-speci "c concepts are given any more weight instructionally than more tangential notions (e.g., Gri $n, Case & Capodilupo, 1995)

That is, it is not simply of concern that teachers may mention rather than teach, but that what gets mentioned may be of questionable importance to building a body ofprincipled conceptual knowledge within any given domain

In several investigations, for example, Alexander and her colleagues (Alexander, Jetton, Kulikowich & Woehler, 1994; Jetton & Alexander, 1997) determined thatteachers often spent instructional time on content that was high in interest value butlow in subject-matter importance
Garner, Gillingham and White, (1989) suitablylabeled these high interest/low importance ideas as `seductive details

aJetton and Alexander (1997), who studied high-school science teachers, concluded that teacherswith strong domain knowledge and, at least, moderate pedagogical knowledge weremore likely to focus on important domain concepts and to convey those conceptse!ectively to students than teachers weak in either domain or pedagogical knowledge

As long as teachers persist in treating content super "cially or devote important instructional time to seductive details rather than to key domain concepts, thenstudents are less likely to form the principled body of subject-matter knowledgeneeded to progress into competence or to demonstrate transfer

Instructional enabling In a review of research on learning environments, Garner (1990) surmised that students more often engage in strategic processing when they are placed in classroomswhere strategice !ort is required and rewarded
Regrettably, Alexander and Knight (1993) argued that many teachers have instituted a practice of instructional enabling

Instructional enabling, according to Alexander and Knight, entails the tacit agree-ment forged between teachers and students whereby students are not academicallychallenged but are given high marks if they perform well on relatively undemandingtasks, display compliance, and behave as good citizens in the classroom

In short, itwould be Alexander and Knight 's contention, and that of others (e.g., Garner, 1990), that classrooms are not particularly academically challenging environments wherestrategice !orts are routinely warranted or rewarded
Even in those instances where teachers have incorporated strategy instruction in their classrooms, presumed strategies are taught more like skills (Alexander, Graham& Harris, 1998a)

That is, students are presented with a strategy, be it domain-speci "c or general, as if it were a fait accompli , a precise set of steps to be executed in just the manner in which they were taught and then ritualistically practiced on a set ofP.A

Such `[s]heer imitation, dictation of steps to be taken, mechanical drill a, as Dewey (1910/1991) warns, `may give results most quickly and yet strengthen traits likely to be fatal to re #ective power a(p

For strategy instruction to contribute to transfer, students must be: (a) shown the value ofsuche !ortful processing; (b) encouraged to modify and personalize the general heuristic; and, (c) provided with opportunities and incentives for such time-consumingand mentally taxing re #ection

Consequently, as long as the incentives for students to personalize strategies or to go beyond the instructional parameters remain limitedand, as long as the time and rewards for strategice !ort are in short supply, transfer either within or across domains is unlikely to be stimulated
Decontextualized and disconnected instruction The phrase `piecemeal ahas been applied to classroom learning (Garner and Alexander, 1989), and appropriately so

The associations that are made in whatstudents learn from one day to the next *to say nothing of one domain to the next or one year to the next *are minimal (e.g., Perkins, 1992; Salomon & Perkins, 1989)

One reason that the "rst author felt strongly about the need for a model of domain learning is that both teachers and their students seemed to move through theeducational experience without any well articulated map for what could or shouldtranspire

Understanding how experts in various "elds think and behave mayo !er a vague picture of what a learner might look like at the end of a long and fruitfuleducational journey (e.g., Chi, Glaser & Farr, 1988; Ericsson & Smith, 1991)
How-ever, it provides little guidance as to how the `endais to be reached and how learners systematically change over the course of such an extended trek

It is not merely that students do not see much of a connection between the world outside of the classroom and what they are learning, although, sadly, this is often thecase (Dewey, 1910/1991; Kolodner, 1997)
The potential relationships between andamong the concepts and procedures students acquire within and across domains arerarely articulated and rarely inferred (Dienes & Berry, 1997)

For this reason, studentscan complete their compulsory educational period with diplomas, and possibly goodgrades, in hand and never appreciate how their learning serves any goal other than thecompletion of the next assignment or the passing of the next exam

Certainly, studentshave little opportunity to become enculturated into these academic domains *to see biology with the eyes of a biologist or to experience history as an historian (Ball, 1993;VanSledright, 1996)
Instead, they think as students who acquire bodies of inertknowledge that retain their viability only for as long as they are needed to satisfy someimmediate and short-lived tasks (Whitehead, 1957)
Why we, as educational researchers, are so surprised that transfer does not occur more often or that students have not formed a disposition toward transfer is a conun-drum
Students are merely exemplifying the very behaviors that are commonlymodeled and routinely reinforced

Periodic training, even whene !ectively devised and delivered, is not likely to transform the habits of the mind (James, 1890) that have beenformed and reinforced over hundreds, and potentially thousands, of instructionalepisodes.570P.A
Nurturing transfer In light of the aforementioned barriers to transfer, several alterations to learning environments should be made that will enhance the likelihood of transfer
First andforemost, a domain-speci "c perspective should be taken to the problem of transfer
This is important because the seeds of transfer are more likely to take root when thosein the classroom community see themselves as progressing toward competence inspeci"c"elds of study
As with apprenticeship models of learning (e.g., Brown & Campione, 1990; Rogo !, 1990), the goal is more long-term than the next assign- ment, the next test, or the next report card

Teachers and students share in theobjective of `rooted relevance a(Alexander et al., 1996) whereby schooled information is not only meaningfully connected to learners and their worlds outside of theclassroom, but also to the fundamental concepts and procedures that de "ne particular domains or disciplines (Ball, 1993, Bereiter, 1995; diSessa, 1989)

Also, understanding the roles that analogical reasoning, in general, and transfer, in particular, play in this journey toward emerging competence helps to give students ' purpose to suche !ortful processing (Holyoak & Thagard, 1997)

That is to say, the following changes, nested within a domain-speci "c framework, may stimulate know- ledge and strategy development in students, and may contribute to students 'personal investment in the target domain

Moreover, these suggestions may give rise toa classroom context where learning is challenging, knowledge and knowing arevalued, and the forging of associations across tasks and contexts is practiced andprized
Stage a three-pronged attack Our"rst recommendation is a general admonition to those who care about transfer
As is evident to many who labor in the "eld of applied psychology, the problem of transfer is multifaceted

It is not a question of whethere !orts should be focused on the learner, the task, orthe context (Marini & Genereux, 1995), or whether the solution to the transfer problem rests in knowledge, strategy, ormotivational training
All are parts of the problem and, consequently, parts of the solution

Toassume that any training program that attends only to one of these elements or thatonly temporarilyo !sets the prevailing educational forces that deter transfer will somehow transform those who rarely or non-spontaneously evidence cross-task andcross-domain reasoning seems delusional

Dispositions toward transfer (Bereiter, 1995), at a minimum, require a rich and cohesive body of domain knowledge, a well-honed strategic repertoire, as well asa personal investment in or identi "cation with an academic domain
These seeds, unlike Jack 's magic beans, cannot spring forth overnight into some monumental structure capable of transporting students into the realm of transfer
Only a long-termcommitment to nurturing all three of these seeds has any real hope of producingstudents with a propensity toward transfer
This three-pronged approach must also be tailored to "t the inter-individual and intra-individual di !erences that exist at varying stages in their academic developmentP.A

For instance, students who are acclimated with regard to a particular domain are understandably more reliant onconditions within the immediate context to stimulate their involvement or to promotetheir learning
These acclimated learners are also more in need of a foundation ofrelevant subject matter knowledge upon which to base subsequent development(Alexander, 1997)

As cluster-analytic studies have shown, there are also those who project varying con"gurations of knowledge, interest, and strategic processing that may necessitate di!ering instructional responses (e.g., Recker & Pirolli, 1995; Renkl, 1997)

For example, those like theE !ortful Processors pro "led in Alexander and Murphy (1998b) may require particular attention to their strategic processing by learning howto apply strategiese !ectively ande $ciently
Nonstrategic Readers, in contrast, may need assistance in recognizing the merits of purposeful strategic engagement to theircontinued academic development
Stri ve for principled understanding Those who study transfer frequently proclaim the power of knowledge (e.g., Byrnes, 1996; Corkill & Fager, 1995; Schunn & Dunbar, 1996)
Yet, educators must notmistake a simple accumulation of knowledge with the call for principled knowledgemade here
What is required is a cohesive body of knowledge that can serve as ananchor for cross-task or cross-domain transfer (Murphy & Woods, 1996)
Whenstudents possess principled knowledge in a domain, the central concepts within thisdomain can function as the source or grounding for analogical reasoning

First, educators guiding students 'domain learning must know their "elds well enough to make thoughtful decisions about what concepts and procedures shouldbecome the centerpieces of classroom instruction (Alexander et al., 1996)
This is astrue for those teaching young children as those working with the upper grades
Importantknowledge and skills must be placed center stage during instruction, with moretangential content appropriately given only minor or cameo roles
When educatorsrecognize the relative value of domain knowledge, they may be more likely to conveythe importance of this knowledge to their students

Further, when teachers havea principled understanding of a domain, they have a focal point in their instruction.Therefore, they may be more inclined to make linkages among concepts and to relatesubsequent content to those key principles, thereby modeling the processes andillustrating the signi "cance of transfer
Second, if they strive for principled understanding, educators must set aside any inclination to mention rather than teach
Perhaps, as diSessa (1989) recommends,teachers should adopt the agenda of teaching more about less
With su $cient instructional time to play with key concepts, teachers may be better able to addressthe individual di !erences found within the classroom
When educators are free to teach more about less they can also revisit central notions under varying conditions572P.A
